claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Oct6 expression was abnormally upregulated in Tead1 cKO at P50.
claims.source: Western blotting of P50 SN lysates showed minimal expression of Oct6 in WT, but abnormally upregulated expression in Tead1 cKO (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: At P50, Oct6 was expressed in ~80% of Tead1 cKO Schwann cell nuclei.
claims.source: Immunohistochemistry of P50 cKO SNs also showed intense Oct6 expression in ~80% of SC nuclei; Oct6 expression was minimal in WT (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: At both P11 and P50, a similar percentage of Schwann cells expressed Krox20 in Tead1 cKO as in WT sciatic nerves.
claims.source: Notably, at both P11 and P50, a similar percentage of SCs expressed Krox20 in Tead1 cKO, as in WT SNs (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Krox20 was upregulated >fourfold in Tead1 cKO compared to WT in Western blots.
claims.source: In Western blots, Krox20 was upregulated >fourfold in cKO compared to WT (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Each Schwann cell in adult Tead1 cKO contains ~twofold more Krox20 than WT.
claims.source: As adult Tead1 cKO mice contain ~twofold more SCs than WT (Figure 3A), these data suggest that each SC in Tead1 cKO contains ~twofold more Krox20 than WT.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the Western blot data and SC counts.

claims.claim: TEAD1 is dispensable for YAP/TAZ to upregulate Krox20.
claims.source: Thus, in contrast to SCs lacking YAP/TAZ, SCs lacking TEAD1 upregulate Krox20, suggesting that TEAD1 is dispensable for YAP/TAZ to upregulate Krox20.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of Krox20 expression in Tead1 cKO vs Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO.

claims.claim: Expression of myelin basic protein (MBP) was abundant in WT P50 sciatic nerves.
claims.source: Consistent with the idea that Krox20 is pivotal for myelin gene transcription, expression of myelin basic protein (MBP), and myelin protein zero (MPZ), was abundant in WT P50 SNs (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Expression of myelin protein zero (MPZ) was abundant in WT P50 sciatic nerves.
claims.source: Consistent with the idea that Krox20 is pivotal for myelin gene transcription, expression of myelin basic protein (MBP), and myelin protein zero (MPZ), was abundant in WT P50 SNs (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Both MBP and MPZ were markedly decreased in Tead1 cKO despite ample expression of Krox20.
claims.source: In contrast, despite ample expression of Krox20, both MBP and MPZ were markedly decreased in Tead1 cKO, indicating that Krox20 fails to properly upregulate myelin proteins without TEAD1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Krox20 fails to properly upregulate myelin proteins without TEAD1.
claims.source: In contrast, despite ample expression of Krox20, both MBP and MPZ were markedly decreased in Tead1 cKO, indicating that Krox20 fails to properly upregulate myelin proteins without TEAD1.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Krox20 is present but myelin proteins are reduced in Tead1 cKO.

claims.claim: Loss of Krox20 or its co-factors, Nab1/2, causes Schwann cells to remain aberrantly in the cell-cycle.
claims.source: To exclude the possibility that Krox20 expressed in cKO SCs is defective, we took advantage of the earlier finding that loss of Krox20 or its co-factors, Nab1/2, causes SCs to remain aberrantly in the cell-cycle (Le et al., 2005b; Zorick et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Only a few EdU-positive Schwann cells exhibited even minimal Krox20 immunoreactivity in either WT or Tead1 cKO at P11.
claims.source: We found that, although ~65% of SC nuclei contained Krox20, only a few EdU-positive SCs exhibited even minimal Krox20 immunoreactivity in either WT or Tead1 cKO (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-staining for EdU and Krox20 shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: TEAD1 is dispensable for Krox20 upregulation but required for Krox20 to upregulate transcription of myelin proteins during development.
claims.source: Thus, despite high levels of functional Krox20, myelin protein expression was greatly reduced in cKO SCs, suggesting that TEAD1 is dispensable for Krox20 upregulation but required for Krox20 to upregulate transcription of myelin proteins during development.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Krox20 is functional but myelin proteins are reduced in Tead1 cKO.

claims.claim: De novo biosynthesis of fatty acids and cholesterol is crucially important for Schwann cells to initiate myelination and to grow a myelin sheath.
claims.source: De novo biosynthesis of fatty acids (integral building blocks of lipids) and cholesterol is crucially important for SCs to initiate myelination and to grow a myelin sheath (Montani et al., 2018; Norrmén et al., 2014; Saher et al., 2009; Verheijen et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: YAP/TAZ may regulate lipid and cholesterol biosynthesis pathways.
claims.source: YAP/TAZ may regulate these pathways, as suggested by reduced mRNA expression in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO of SREBPs TFs (Sterol regulatory element binding proteins) and their target enzymes involved in lipid/cholesterol biosynthesis (Deng et al., 2017; Poitelon et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies showing reduced mRNA expression.

claims.claim: Levels of nuclear SREBP1 were not affected by loss of TEAD1 at P8.
claims.source: Western blot analysis showed that levels of nuclear SREBP1 were not affected by loss of TEAD1 at P8, and only slightly reduced at P40 (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Levels of nuclear SREBP1 were only slightly reduced by loss of TEAD1 at P40.
claims.source: Western blot analysis showed that levels of nuclear SREBP1 were not affected by loss of TEAD1 at P8, and only slightly reduced at P40 (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: SCD1 was reduced in Tead1 cKO at P8, but slightly increased at P40.
claims.source: SCD1 was reduced at P8, but slightly increased at P40.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: SREBP2 was ~50% reduced in Tead1 cKO at both P8 and P40.
claims.source: In contrast to SREBP1, SREBP2 was ~50% reduced in Tead1 cKO at both P8 and P40.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: HMGCR was not reduced in Tead1 cKO at P8 or P40 despite marked reduction in SREBP2.
claims.source: Despite marked reduction in SREBP2, HMGCR was not reduced at P8 or P40.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Both FDPS and IDI1 levels were greatly reduced in Tead1 cKO at both P8 and P40.
claims.source: However, both FDPS and IDI1 levels were greatly reduced at both P8 and P40 (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: SREBP1 levels were unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
claims.source: We found that, as in Tead1 cKO, SREBP1 levels were unaffected and SCD1 levels were markedly increased by the loss of YAP/TAZ in cDKO at P60 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: SCD1 levels were markedly increased in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
claims.source: We found that, as in Tead1 cKO, SREBP1 levels were unaffected and SCD1 levels were markedly increased by the loss of YAP/TAZ in cDKO at P60 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: SREBP2 levels were not markedly reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
claims.source: Unlike in Tead1 cKO, levels of SREBP2 were not markedly reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: HMGCR levels were not reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
claims.source: As in Tead1 cKO, however, HMGCR levels were not reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, whereas levels of FDPS and IDI1 were greatly reduced.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Levels of FDPS and IDI1 were greatly reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO at P60.
claims.source: As in Tead1 cKO, however, HMGCR levels were not reduced in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, whereas levels of FDPS and IDI1 were greatly reduced.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 transcriptional complex selectively upregulates IDI1 and FDPS, contributing to cholesterol biosynthesis.
claims.source: These results therefore indicate that YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 transcriptional complex selectively upregulates IDI1 and FDPS, contributing to cholesterol biosynthesis.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the consistent reduction of FDPS and IDI1 in both Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO.

claims.claim: Reduction in cholesterol biosynthesis may prevent myelin formation and growth in Tead1 cKO.
claims.source: Together with the lack of synthesis of myelin proteins, this reduction in cholesterol biosynthesis may prevent myelin formation and growth in Tead1 cKO.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined defects in myelin protein expression and cholesterol biosynthesis.

claims.claim: Tead1 iKO mice appeared normal without obvious signs of peripheral neuropathy up to 5 months post-tamoxifen.
claims.source: Tead1 iKO mice appeared normal without obvious signs of peripheral neuropathy up to 5 months post-tamoxifen, the longest time of observation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by observation of mice.

claims.claim: TEM analysis of Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves between 3 and 5 months post-tamoxifen revealed some large axons undergoing demyelination or completely demyelinated.
claims.source: TEM analysis of iKO SNs between 3 and 5 months post-tamoxifen revealed, however, some large axons undergoing demyelination or completely demyelinated, which were undetectable in WT SNs (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Demyelinated axons were observed in discrete regions of Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves, indicating segmental demyelination (<5% large axons).
claims.source: The demyelinated axons were observed in discrete regions of SNs, indicating segmental demyelination (<5% large axons on 12 TEM sections exhibiting demyelinated axons).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM observations.

claims.claim: Nerve conduction velocity of Tead1 iKO mice did not significantly differ from that of WT.
claims.source: NCV of these iKO mice did not significantly differ from that of WT (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Loss of TEAD1 in adult Schwann cells evoked only modest focal demyelination in a small number of axons, which did not cause significant functional impairment of peripheral nerves.
claims.source: Therefore, loss of TEAD1 in adult SCs evoked only modest focal demyelination in a small number of axons, which did not cause significant functional impairment of peripheral nerves.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the TEM and NCV data in Tead1 iKO mice.

claims.claim: Many C-fibers in most Remak bundles were not ensheathed by Schwann cell cytoplasm in Tead1 iKO.
claims.source: In stark contrast, in Tead1 iKO, many C-fibers in most Remak bundles were not ensheathed by SC cytoplasm (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Some small Remak bundles were occasionally myelinated in Tead1 iKO.
claims.source: Furthermore, some small Remak bundles were occasionally myelinated (Figure 6E), as in Tead1 cKO SNs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: TEAD1 is required for formation as well as maintenance of Remak bundles.
claims.source: Thus, TEAD1 is required for formation as well as maintenance of Remak bundles.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the Remak bundle defects in both Tead1 cKO and iKO mice.

claims.claim: Krox20 was dramatically downregulated in most Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO Schwann cells only 2 weeks post-tamoxifen.
claims.source: As a control, we injected Plp1-CreER; Yap1fl/fl; Wwtr1fl/fl mice with tamoxifen and reproduced our previous result: Krox20 was dramatically downregulated in most Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SCs only 2 weeks post-tamoxifen (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: In Tead1 iKO, Krox20 expression was indistinguishable from WT even at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen.
claims.source: In contrast, in Tead1 iKO, Krox20 expression was indistinguishable from WT even at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: Oct6 was not elevated in Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves.
claims.source: We then investigated Oct6 expression. Unlike in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SNs (Grove et al., 2017), Oct6 was not elevated in Tead1 iKO SNs (Figure 7C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: TEAD1 is dispensable for maintaining Krox20 expression in adult Schwann cells.
claims.source: Thus, TEAD1 is dispensable for maintaining Krox20 expression in adult SCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the normal Krox20 expression in Tead1 iKO.

claims.claim: The SREBP1 pathway was unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO at 2 weeks post-tamoxifen.
claims.source: Western blotting of WT and Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SN lysates showed that the SREBP1 pathway and expression of SREBP2 and HMGCR in the SREBP2 pathway were unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Expression of SREBP2 and HMGCR in the SREBP2 pathway were unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO at 2 weeks post-tamoxifen.
claims.source: Western blotting of WT and Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SN lysates showed that the SREBP1 pathway and expression of SREBP2 and HMGCR in the SREBP2 pathway were unaffected in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO (Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: FDPS and IDI1 levels were significantly downregulated in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO at 2 weeks post-tamoxifen.
claims.source: However, FDPS and IDI1 levels were significantly downregulated in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO, recapitulating the effect of developmental loss of YAP/TAZ on these proteins (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The acute downregulation of FDPS and IDI1 correlates with the acute demyelination previously observed in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO mice.
claims.source: Thus, the acute downregulation of these key enzymes for cholesterol biosynthesis correlates with the acute demyelination previously observed in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the correlation between enzyme downregulation and demyelination phenotype.

claims.claim: YAP/TAZ maintain myelination through both myelin gene expression and the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway.
claims.source: This result suggests that YAP/TAZ maintain myelination through both myelin gene expression and the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the effects of YAP/TAZ loss on both Krox20 and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.

claims.claim: The SREBP pathways were not significantly affected by loss of TEAD1 in adult Schwann cells.
claims.source: Western blotting of Tead1 iKO SN lysates revealed that the SREBP pathways were not significantly affected by loss of TEAD1 (Figure 7E), unlike Tead1 cKO in which FDPS and IDI1 were markedly downregulated (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: TEAD1 is dispensable for cholesterol synthesis in adult Schwann cells.
claims.source: This result suggests that TEAD1 is dispensable for cholesterol synthesis in adult SCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of effect on SREBP pathways in Tead1 iKO.

claims.claim: YAP/TAZ are not required for axon regeneration but are crucial for remyelination.
claims.source: YAP/TAZ are not required for axon regeneration but are crucial for remyelination (Grove et al., 2017; Jeanette et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO mice die ~2 weeks post-injury.
claims.source: Because Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO mice die ~2 weeks post-injury (wpi), it remains possible that remyelination is delayed rather than completely blocked.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Numerous Tuj1-labeled axons regenerated along the distal nerve stump in Tead1 iKO, as in WT sciatic nerves.
claims.source: Longitudinal sections of iKO SNs showed numerous Tuj1-labeled axons that regenerated along the distal nerve stump, as in WT SNs (Figure 8B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: MBP immunoreactivity was greatly reduced in the distal nerve stump of Tead1 iKO compared to WT.
claims.source: However, MBP immunoreactivity was greatly reduced in the distal nerve stump of Tead1 iKO, compared to WT, suggesting that axons regenerated but were not remyelinated.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8B.

claims.claim: Axons regenerated but were not remyelinated in Tead1 iKO after nerve crush.
claims.source: However, MBP immunoreactivity was greatly reduced in the distal nerve stump of Tead1 iKO, compared to WT, suggesting that axons regenerated but were not remyelinated.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the presence of axons but absence of myelin in Tead1 iKO.

claims.claim: Regenerated axons reached hindlimb muscles and reinnervated neuromuscular junctions in Tead1 iKO, as in WT.
claims.source: We also found that regenerated axons reached hindlimb muscles and reinnervated neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) in iKO, as in WT (Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by NMJ staining shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: Tead1 iKO frequently exhibited features of paralyzed muscles after nerve crush.
claims.source: Moreover, Tead1 iKO frequently exhibited features of paralyzed muscles, such as axon terminals that grew past the synaptic area, fragmented clusters of acetylcholine receptors (AChRs), and satellite extra-synaptic AChRs (Wright et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by NMJ staining shown in Figure 8C and citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Semithin and EM analysis confirmed virtual absence of myelinated axons in Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves after nerve crush.
claims.source: Semithin and EM analysis confirmed virtual absence of myelinated axons in iKO SNs; although large axons were associated with SCs, they were not myelinated (Figure 8D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by semi-thin and TEM data shown in Figure 8D.

claims.claim: Electrical stimulation of Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves did not elicit CMAPs or NCV after nerve crush.
claims.source: Accordingly, electrical stimulation of iKO SNs did not elicit CMAPs or NCV (Figure 8E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 8E.

claims.claim: TEAD1 in Schwann cells is not required for axon regeneration but is required for remyelination after nerve injury.
claims.source: Thus, like YAP/TAZ, TEAD1 in SCs is not required for axon regeneration but is required for remyelination after nerve injury.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the nerve crush experiments in Tead1 iKO mice.

claims.claim: A similar percentage of Schwann cells were in S-phase in both WT and Tead1 iKO sciatic nerves at 3 days post-injury.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis of SC proliferation at 3 dpi by counting EdU+/Sox10+ SCs showed that a similar percentage of SCs were in S-phase in both WT and Tead1 iKO SNs (Figure 8F), suggesting that, like YAP/TAZ (Grove et al., 2017), TEAD1 is not required for proliferation of repair SCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EdU staining shown in Figure 8F.

claims.claim: TEAD1 is not required for proliferation of repair Schwann cells.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis of SC proliferation at 3 dpi by counting EdU+/Sox10+ SCs showed that a similar percentage of SCs were in S-phase in both WT and Tead1 iKO SNs (Figure 8F), suggesting that, like YAP/TAZ (Grove et al., 2017), TEAD1 is not required for proliferation of repair SCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the similar proliferation rates in WT and Tead1 iKO after injury.

claims.claim: Krox20 was upregulated in Tead1 iKO Schwann cells at 4 weeks post-injury, as in WT Schwann cells.
claims.source: Notably, in contrast to Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO SCs, which fail to upregulate Krox20 after injury (Grove et al., 2017), Krox20 was upregulated in Tead1 iKO SCs, as in WT SCs (Figure 8G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8G.

claims.claim: Oct6 was aberrantly elevated in Tead1 iKO Schwann cells at 4 weeks post-injury.
claims.source: Furthermore, Oct6 was aberrantly elevated in Tead1 iKO SCs, like in Tead1 cKO SCs during development (Figure 8H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 8H.

claims.claim: Remyelination requires TEAD1 for Oct6 downregulation and for Krox20 to upregulate myelin proteins.
claims.source: These results suggest that, similar to developmental myelination, remyelination requires TEAD1 for Oct6 downregulation and for Krox20 to upregulate myelin proteins.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of molecular phenotypes between developmental and regenerative myelination in Tead1 mutants.

claims.claim: Almost complete absence of remyelination at 4 weeks post-injury highlights the non-redundant, crucial role of TEAD1 in the remyelination of regenerating nerves after injury.
claims.source: Additionally, almost complete absence of remyelination at 4 wpi highlights the non-redundant, crucial role of TEAD1 in the remyelination of regenerating nerves after injury.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the severe remyelination defect in Tead1 iKO after nerve crush.

claims.claim: TEAD1 is a crucial transcription factor mediating myelin formation, growth, and regeneration.
claims.source: The present study conclusively establishes TEAD1 as a crucial TF mediating myelin formation, growth, and regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: TEAD1 is critical in the proper formation and maintenance of Remak bundles.
claims.source: Our findings also suggest that TEAD1 is critical in the proper formation and maintenance of Remak bundles.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim based on the Remak bundle data in Tead1 cKO and iKO mice.

claims.claim: Tead1 cKO mice grossly phenocopy Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO mice.
claims.source: Although SCs express other TEADs, Tead1 cKO mice grossly phenocopy Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO mice.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of phenotypes between the two mutants.

claims.claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibit abnormal Schwann cell proliferation.
claims.source: They exhibit abnormal SC proliferation, delayed radial sorting, blocked myelin formation and remyelination, and normal axon regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the proliferation data presented earlier.

claims.claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibit delayed radial sorting.
claims.source: They exhibit abnormal SC proliferation, delayed radial sorting, blocked myelin formation and remyelination, and normal axon regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the radial sorting data presented earlier.

claims.claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibit blocked myelin formation and remyelination.
claims.source: They exhibit abnormal SC proliferation, delayed radial sorting, blocked myelin formation and remyelination, and normal axon regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the myelination data presented earlier.

claims.claim: Tead1 cKO mice exhibit normal axon regeneration.
claims.source: They exhibit abnormal SC proliferation, delayed radial sorting, blocked myelin formation and remyelination, and normal axon regeneration.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the axon regeneration data presented earlier.

claims.claim: YAP/TAZ regulate both Schwann cell proliferation and differentiation by partnering mainly with TEAD1 for developmental myelination and remyelination after injury.
claims.source: These similarities show that YAP/TAZ regulate both SC proliferation and differentiation, the two opposing processes crucial for myelination, by partnering mainly with TEAD1 for developmental myelination and remyelination after injury.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the similarity of phenotypes between Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO.

claims.claim: Unlike Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, Tead1 cKO initiates myelin formation in some developing axons.
claims.source: Unlike Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, Tead1 cKO initiates myelin formation in some developing axons and maintains myelination in almost all adult axons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of myelination phenotypes between the two mutants.

claims.claim: Tead1 cKO maintains myelination in almost all adult axons.
claims.source: Unlike Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, Tead1 cKO initiates myelin formation in some developing axons and maintains myelination in almost all adult axons.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the Tead1 iKO data showing minimal demyelination.

claims.claim: In Tead1 cKO, Krox20 is upregulated and a large excess of Schwann cells is generated.
claims.source: Additionally, in Tead1 cKO, Krox20 is upregulated and a large excess of SCs is generated.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the Krox20 and SC number data presented earlier.

claims.claim: Whereas some developing axons are myelinated in Tead1 cKO, almost all axons regenerating after injury are unmyelinated.
claims.source: It is also notable that, whereas some developing axons are myelinated in Tead1 cKO, almost all axons regenerating after injury are unmyelinated.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of developmental and regenerative myelination in Tead1 cKO.

claims.claim: The differences between Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO are likely due to stage-dependent redundancy and opposing roles of TEADs.
claims.source: These differences are likely due to stage-dependent redundancy and opposing roles of TEADs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the phenotypic differences and the known expression of multiple TEADs.

claims.claim: Other TEADs can retain nuclear YAP/TAZ, thereby supporting transcriptional activity of YAP/TAZ, but cannot substitute for some or most of the functions of TEAD1 in a stage-dependent manner.
claims.source: Thus, other TEADs can retain nuclear YAP/TAZ, thereby supporting transcriptional activity of YAP/TAZ, but cannot substitute for some or most of the functions of TEAD1 in a stage-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ in Tead1 mutants and the phenotypic differences from Yap1/Wwtr1 mutants.

claims.claim: The unique roles of TEAD1 change dynamically in successive steps of myelination, even though other TEADs are present.
claims.source: It is also notable that, like YAP/TAZ, the unique roles of TEAD1 change dynamically in successive steps of myelination, even though other TEADs are present.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the different phenotypes at different developmental stages.

claims.claim: TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of Schwann cells.
claims.source: Thus, TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of SCs; uniquely opposes SC proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting; redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20; and then uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the proliferation data at P3.

claims.claim: TEAD1 uniquely opposes Schwann cell proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting.
claims.source: Thus, TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of SCs; uniquely opposes SC proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting; redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20; and then uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the proliferation data at P22.

claims.claim: TEAD1 redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20.
claims.source: Thus, TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of SCs; uniquely opposes SC proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting; redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20; and then uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the Krox20 data showing normal upregulation in Tead1 cKO.

claims.claim: TEAD1 uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
claims.source: Thus, TEAD1 is uniquely required for timely proliferation of SCs; uniquely opposes SC proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting; redundantly promotes upregulation of Krox20; and then uniquely promotes upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the myelin protein and cholesterol biosynthesis data.

claims.claim: YAP-TEAD4 can substitute for YAP-TEAD1 in upregulating transcription from the Krox20 promoter, but not from the MPZ intronic enhancer.
claims.source: Such unique and redundant roles for TEAD1 in the presence of other TEADs are supported by cell-based transcription assays, in which YAP-TEAD4 can substitute for YAP-TEAD1 in upregulating transcription from the Krox20 promoter, but not from the MPZ intronic enhancer (Fernando et al., 2016).

results.result: TEAD1 is efficiently deleted in Tead1 cKO Schwann cells, with TEAD1 expressed in 100% of WT Schwann cells at P22 but undetectable in >97% of Tead1 cKO Schwann cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C47 and C48 are directly supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A, demonstrating efficient Cre-mediated deletion of TEAD1 in the conditional knockout model. This establishes the validity of the genetic model for subsequent experiments.

results.result: Loss of TEAD1 does not affect nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ in Schwann cells, presumably due to retention by other TEADs.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1D showing nuclear YAP/TAZ in Tead1 cKO. Claim C50 is a reasonable inference given that multiple TEADs are expressed in Schwann cells and can bind YAP/TAZ. This finding is important for interpreting the functional relationship between TEAD1 and YAP/TAZ.

results.result: Tead1 cKO mice exhibit severe peripheral neuropathy phenotype including reduced size, labored breathing, and splayed limbs, requiring euthanasia before P60.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 are supported by observational data in Figure 2A and Video 1. The interpretation of severe peripheral neuropathy (C54) is consistent with the observed phenotypes and is validated by subsequent electrophysiological and histological analyses. C55 is a procedural statement.

results.result: Tead1 cKO sciatic nerves show reduced myelin content and severely impaired nerve conduction velocity (~8 m/s vs ~40 m/s in WT).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by gross morphology (Figure 2B) and electrophysiology data (Figure 2D). The ~5-fold reduction in NCV is substantial and statistically significant, providing functional evidence of the myelination defect. The measurements appear technically sound with appropriate controls.

results.result: Myelination in Tead1 cKO is arrested rather than delayed, with radial sorting delayed but not blocked at P3, largely unmyelinated nerves at P22 that remain unchanged at P50, and no significant increase in myelin thickness between P22 and P50.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 are supported by TEM and semi-thin section data at multiple time points (Figures 2E-H). The g-ratio measurements (C63) provide quantitative evidence that myelin thickness does not improve over time, supporting the interpretation of arrested rather than delayed myelination (C65). The longitudinal analysis strengthens this conclusion.

results.result: The myelination defect in Tead1 cKO affects axons of all diameters but is particularly notable in larger diameter axons, and mean axon diameter is reduced at P22 but increases with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by g-ratio scatter plots (Figures 2I-J) and axon diameter measurements (Figure 2K). The analysis appropriately examines the relationship between axon diameter and myelination defect. The observation that axon diameter increases with age despite persistent myelination defects is important for understanding the phenotype.

results.result: TEAD1 is required for proper formation of Remak bundles, with ~80% of C-fibers not ensheathed by Schwann cell cytoplasm in P50 Tead1 cKO sciatic nerves.
results.evaluation: Claims C69, C11, and C147 are supported by TEM analysis and quantification (Figure 2L-M). This represents a novel finding regarding TEAD1's role in non-myelinating Schwann cells. The quantification is rigorous and the phenotype is distinct from radial sorting defects, as discussed in the manuscript.

results.result: TEAD1 is required for optimal Schwann cell proliferation during early development, with Schwann cell number reduced to about half of WT at P3 and greatly reduced numbers of Ki67+ and EdU+ cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 are supported by cell counting and proliferation marker data (Figures 3A-C). The measurements are quantitative and statistically significant. This establishes TEAD1's role in promoting early SC proliferation, which is important for understanding the biphasic proliferation phenotype.

results.result: TEAD1 has a biphasic effect on Schwann cell proliferation: promoting proliferation early (P3) but opposing it later (P22-P50), with Schwann cell numbers becoming more than twice WT levels at P22 and P50, and this switch is required for timely cell-cycle exit and differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by longitudinal proliferation data (Figures 3A-D). The demonstration that increased proliferation at P22 is not due to residual TEAD1+ cells (C75) is important for interpretation. The biphasic effect is a key finding, though the molecular mechanism underlying the switch is not fully elucidated. The inference about cell-cycle exit (C76) is reasonable given the established relationship between proliferation and differentiation.

results.result: Oct6 expression is abnormally upregulated in Tead1 cKO Schwann cells at P50, with minimal expression in WT but expression in ~80% of cKO Schwann cell nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are supported by Western blot (Figure 4A) and immunohistochemistry (Figure 4B) data. The persistent Oct6 expression is significant because Oct6 should normally be downregulated after Krox20 upregulation. This finding is important for understanding the differentiation block.

results.result: TEAD1 is dispensable for Krox20 upregulation but required for Krox20 to upregulate myelin proteins, with similar percentages of Krox20+ Schwann cells in Tead1 cKO and WT but >4-fold increase in total Krox20 protein levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C88 are supported by immunohistochemistry (Figure 4C) and Western blot (Figure 4A) data. The calculation that each SC contains ~2-fold more Krox20 (C87) is a reasonable inference from the Western blot data and SC counts. This is a key mechanistic finding distinguishing TEAD1 from YAP/TAZ function and establishing that TEAD1 acts downstream or in parallel to Krox20 upregulation.

results.result: Despite ample Krox20 expression, myelin proteins MBP and MPZ are markedly decreased in Tead1 cKO, indicating that Krox20 fails to properly upregulate myelin proteins without TEAD1.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C92 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 4A). This is a critical finding establishing that TEAD1 is required for Krox20 function. The inference (C92) is well-supported by the data showing dissociation between Krox20 levels and myelin protein expression.

results.result: Krox20 expressed in Tead1 cKO Schwann cells is functional, as evidenced by the fact that only a few EdU+ Schwann cells show Krox20 immunoreactivity, consistent with Krox20's known role in promoting cell-cycle exit.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C94 are supported by co-staining data (Figure 4D) and citation to previous work. This control experiment is important for excluding the possibility that Krox20 protein in cKO is non-functional. The logic is sound: if Krox20 were defective, it would not suppress proliferation.

results.result: TEAD1 selectively regulates cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes FDPS and IDI1, which are greatly reduced in Tead1 cKO at both P8 and P40, while SREBP1 and HMGCR are not consistently affected.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C103 are supported by Western blot data at two time points (Figure 5A). The selective effect on FDPS and IDI1 but not HMGCR is important for understanding the mechanism. The temporal analysis (P8 and P40) strengthens the conclusion that this is not simply due to developmental delay.

results.result: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 transcriptional complex selectively upregulates IDI1 and FDPS in cholesterol biosynthesis, with similar selective reduction of these enzymes in Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO as in Tead1 cKO.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 are supported by Western blot data from Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO (Figure 5B). The parallel findings in both mutants strongly support the conclusion that YAP/TAZ and TEAD1 function together to regulate these specific enzymes. This is important mechanistic evidence.

results.result: Loss of TEAD1 in adult Schwann cells causes only modest focal demyelination in a small number of axons (<5%) without significant functional impairment, as evidenced by normal NCV in Tead1 iKO mice up to 5 months post-tamoxifen.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C115 are supported by observational data, TEM analysis (Figure 6B), and NCV measurements (Figure 6C). The finding that TEAD1 is largely dispensable for myelin maintenance contrasts with its requirement for myelin formation, suggesting stage-dependent functions. The quantification of affected axons and functional assessment strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: TEAD1 is required for maintenance of Remak bundles in adult nerves, with many C-fibers not ensheathed in Tead1 iKO and occasional aberrant myelination of small Remak bundles.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C118 are supported by TEM data (Figures 6D-E). The finding that TEAD1 is required for both formation and maintenance of Remak bundles is important and consistent with the developmental phenotype. This establishes a continuous requirement for TEAD1 in non-myelinating Schwann cells.

results.result: TEAD1 is dispensable for maintaining Krox20 expression in adult Schwann cells, with Krox20 expression indistinguishable from WT in Tead1 iKO at 6 weeks post-tamoxifen, contrasting with dramatic Krox20 downregulation in Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO at 2 weeks.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C122 are supported by immunostaining data (Figures 7A-C). The comparison with Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO is important for understanding the differential requirements for TEAD1 vs YAP/TAZ in myelin maintenance. This finding helps explain why Tead1 iKO has a milder demyelination phenotype.

results.result: In adult Schwann cells, acute loss of YAP/TAZ causes significant downregulation of FDPS and IDI1 at 2 weeks post-tamoxifen, correlating with acute demyelination, suggesting YAP/TAZ maintain myelination through both myelin gene expression and cholesterol biosynthesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 are supported by Western blot data from Yap1/Wwtr1 iDKO (Figure 7D). The temporal correlation between enzyme downregulation and demyelination is suggestive but not definitive proof of causation. The inference about dual mechanisms (C127) is reasonable but somewhat speculative without direct functional rescue experiments.

results.result: TEAD1 is dispensable for cholesterol synthesis in adult Schwann cells, with SREBP pathways not significantly affected by loss of TEAD1 in Tead1 iKO, unlike the marked downregulation of FDPS and IDI1 in developmental Tead1 cKO.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are supported by Western blot data (Figure 7E) and comparison with developmental data. This stage-dependent difference is important for understanding why myelin maintenance is less affected than myelin formation in TEAD1 mutants. The inference is well-supported by the data.

results.result: TEAD1 is not required for axon regeneration but is absolutely required for remyelination after nerve injury, with numerous regenerated axons reaching muscles and reinnervating NMJs but virtual absence of myelinated axons and no detectable CMAPs or NCV at 4 weeks post-injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C139 are supported by comprehensive analysis including immunostaining (Figure 8B), NMJ analysis (Figure 8C), TEM (Figure 8D), and electrophysiology (Figure 8E). The dissociation between axon regeneration and remyelination is clearly demonstrated. The functional consequences are severe, establishing TEAD1 as crucial for regenerative myelination.

results.result: TEAD1 is not required for proliferation of repair Schwann cells, with similar percentages of EdU+ Schwann cells in WT and Tead1 iKO at 3 days post-injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C140-C141 are supported by EdU incorporation data (Figure 8F). This finding is important for understanding that TEAD1's role in remyelination is not due to defective repair SC proliferation, paralleling the YAP/TAZ phenotype. The timing of analysis (3 dpi) is appropriate for assessing repair SC proliferation.

results.result: Remyelination requires TEAD1 for Oct6 downregulation and for Krox20 to upregulate myelin proteins, with Krox20 upregulated but Oct6 aberrantly elevated in Tead1 iKO Schwann cells at 4 weeks post-injury.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 are supported by immunostaining data (Figures 8G-H). The molecular phenotype parallels that seen in developmental myelination, supporting the inference (C144) that similar mechanisms operate in both contexts. This strengthens the overall model of TEAD1 function.

results.result: Tead1 cKO mice grossly phenocopy Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO mice in exhibiting abnormal Schwann cell proliferation, delayed radial sorting, blocked myelin formation and remyelination, and normal axon regeneration, establishing TEAD1 as a major partner of YAP/TAZ.
results.evaluation: Claims C148-C153 are supported by comprehensive comparison of phenotypes throughout the manuscript. The similarities are substantial and well-documented. However, important differences also exist (e.g., Krox20 upregulation, some myelin formation in cKO), which are appropriately discussed. The conclusion that TEAD1 is a major partner is well-supported.

results.result: Unlike Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO, Tead1 cKO initiates myelin formation in some developing axons, maintains myelination in almost all adult axons, upregulates Krox20, generates excess Schwann cells, and shows differential effects on developmental vs regenerative myelination.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C157 are supported by data throughout the manuscript comparing Tead1 cKO with Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO. These differences are important for understanding TEAD redundancy and stage-dependent functions. The observations are well-documented, though the molecular basis for these differences requires further investigation.

results.result: The differences between Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 cDKO are likely due to stage-dependent redundancy and opposing roles of TEADs, with other TEADs retaining nuclear YAP/TAZ but unable to fully substitute for TEAD1 functions in a stage-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C160 are supported by the phenotypic differences, nuclear YAP/TAZ localization data (Figure 1D), and expression of multiple TEADs (Figure 1B). The inference about redundancy and stage-dependence is reasonable given the data, though direct functional evidence for other TEADs' roles would strengthen this conclusion. The model is consistent with TEAD biology in other systems.

results.result: TEAD1 has dynamic, stage-dependent roles in myelination: uniquely required for timely SC proliferation early, uniquely opposing proliferation to promote cell-cycle exit after radial sorting, redundantly promoting Krox20 upregulation, and uniquely promoting upregulation of myelin proteins and cholesterol biosynthetic enzymes.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C164 synthesize findings from multiple experiments throughout the manuscript. Each component is supported by specific data: proliferation (Figures 3A-C), cell-cycle exit (Figures 3A-D), Krox20 (Figure 4C), myelin proteins (Figure 4A), and cholesterol enzymes (Figure 5A). This represents a comprehensive model of TEAD1 function, though some aspects (particularly the redundancy in Krox20 upregulation) are inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Some Tead1 cKO Schwann cells can initiate myelination but fail to grow myelin sheaths proportional to axon diameter, and TEADs 1 and 4 may oppose each other in regulating myelin sheath growth and Schwann cell proliferation.
results.evaluation: Claim C169 is supported by g-ratio data. Claim C170 is supported by the high efficiency of TEAD1 deletion. Claims C171-C173 are more speculative, based on comparison with published TEAD4 cKO data showing opposite phenotypes. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by citation, direct experimental evidence of TEAD4 function in this study would strengthen these claims.

results.result: TEAD1 functions redundantly in Krox20 upregulation but is required for Krox20 to promote myelination, possibly through direct co-activation with Krox20 or by preventing Oct6-mediated repression of Krox20 activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C174-C176 are well-supported by the data. However, claims C177-C181 are largely speculative mechanistic hypotheses. While the speculation is reasonable and supported by citations to relevant literature, direct experimental evidence for the proposed mechanisms (Oct6 repression vs. co-activation) is lacking. Additional experiments such as ChIP-seq, reporter assays, or rescue experiments would be needed to distinguish between these possibilities.

results.result: Fatty acid synthesis is not directly regulated by TEAD1 or YAP/TAZ, but cholesterol biosynthesis is defective in Tead1 cKO and Yap1/Wwtr1 mutants, with phenotypes similar to SCAP cKO and Squalene synthase cKO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C189-C191 are supported by Western blot data showing selective effects on cholesterol but not fatty acid biosynthetic enzymes. Claims C192-C195 are supported by citations to previous studies showing similar phenotypes in other lipid biosynthesis mutants. The comparison strengthens the interpretation that cholesterol biosynthesis defects contribute to the myelination phenotype.

results.result: YAP/TAZ-TEAD1 regulation of FDPS and IDI1 may occur through direct transcriptional regulation rather than through mTORC1, based on phenotypic differences between Tead1 cKO and Raptor cKO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C200 are supported by citations to previous studies. Claim C201 is a reasonable inference from the phenotypic differences, but the evidence is indirect. Claim C202 is speculative. Claim C203 is supported by citation. While the argument against mTORC1 as an intermediary is reasonable, direct evidence for transcriptional regulation (e.g., ChIP data showing TEAD1 binding to FDPS/IDI1 promoters) would be needed to definitively support this mechanism.

results.result: The defective Schwann cell ensheathment of C-fibers in Tead1 mutants is distinct from radial sorting defects and not due to developmental delay, and TEAD1 may mediate extracellular signaling from basal lamina and/or axons required for proper C-fiber ensheathment.
results.evaluation: Claims C204-C210 are supported by TEM data and citations to previous studies. The distinction from radial sorting defects is well-argued. Claim C211 is speculative but reasonable given the comparison with other mutants affecting basal lamina or NRG1 signaling. However, direct evidence for the proposed signaling mechanism is lacking. The speculation is appropriately presented as a hypothesis for future investigation.
